units.title: Scale and Measuring Distance and Area
units.intro: In this unit you learn to make a scale, find the distance along a curved path, and find areas on a map using its scale.

area.title: A square and a rectangle on a map

cards.title: What is a scale?
body: A **scale** is the relationship between a **map distance** and a **ground distance**.
It is a **ratio**. All maps have scales. You need a scale to draw a map.

cards.title: Why do we need a scale?
body: If a scale is given:
- you can find the **ground distance** along a straight or a curved path;
- you can calculate the **areas** of places on a map.

cards.title: Example 1: a scale for a classroom
cards.problem: A classroom is 2 metres by 4 metres. Make a scale and draw it on paper.

steps.text: The sides 2 m and 4 m are **ground distances**. They are too big for paper.
Say **1 cm** on the paper stands for **2 m** on the ground.
Draw a rectangle 1 cm by 2 cm.

cards.answer: The scale is 1 cm to 2 metres.

cards.title: Example 2: a football ground
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Ground
states.text: The football ground is **120 m by 60 m**. These are ground distances. It is too large for paper.

states.label: Paper
states.text: Let **10 cm** stand for 120 m. Then 60 m is **5 cm**. Draw a rectangle 10 cm by 5 cm.

states.label: Scale
states.text: 120 m ÷ 10 = 12 m. So **1 cm on the map stands for 12 metres**. The scale is **1 cm to 12 metres**.

cards.title: Try it: a scale for 400 km
cards.problem: On Figure 1.4 the line A–B is drawn. The ground distance is 400 km. Suppose the line is 8 cm long on your paper. What is the scale?

steps.text: Map distance = 8 cm. Ground distance = 400 km.
So 1 cm stands for 50 km.

cards.answer: 1 cm to 50 km (with an 8 cm line).

cards.title: Memory trick: M before G

letters.m: small, in cm, measured with a ruler
big, in m or km, the real distance

body: A scale always says **Map** first, then **Ground**: "1 cm (map) to 12 m (ground)".

cards.q: 120 m is shown as 10 cm. What is the scale?
cards.why: 120 m ÷ 10 = 12 m. So 1 cm on the map stands for 12 m on the ground.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Scale = map distance compared with ground distance.
To make a scale: choose a map length, then divide the ground distance by it.

cards.title: Straight and curved
body: With the scale of a map you can find the distance of a **straight line**.
You can also find the distance of a **curved path**, such as a road or a railway.

steps.text: **1.** Use a **ruler** to measure the map distance between X and Y.
**2.** The map distance is **6 cm**.
**3–4.** The scale is 1 cm to 3 km. So 6 cm is 6 × 3 = **18 km** on the ground.

cards.title: The calculation
cards.problem: Map distance 6 cm. Scale 1 cm to 3 km. Find the ground distance.

cards.title: B. Along a curved path
body: A ruler is hard to use on a curved path, because the path is not straight.
Use a **pair of dividers** or a **piece of string**.
You need two things: the **map distance** and the **scale**.

steps.text: **1.** Divide the curved line A–B with light pencil marks into sections that are nearly straight.
**2.** Measure each section carefully with the pair of dividers.
**3.** Join the sections into one straight line on a piece of paper.
**4–5.** Measure the whole line: **10 cm**. Convert with the scale 1 cm to 3 km: 10 × 3 = **30 km**.
**1–2.** Make a **knot** at one end of the string. Put the knot at A.
**3.** Follow the curved line with the string up to B.
Put the knot at **0** on a ruler. Measure the string: **10 cm**. This is the map distance.
**5.** Convert: 10 cm is **30 km** on the ground.

cards.title: Which way is easier?
body: Using a piece of string is **much simpler**. It does not take much time.

cards.title: Three tools
body: Tap each dot to see the tool and when to use it.

cards.title: Try it: 8 cm at 1 cm to 12 km
cards.problem: The scale of a map is 1 cm to 12 km. The map distance between two places is 8 cm. What is the ground distance?

cards.q: Map distance 5 cm, scale 1 cm to 4 km. Ground distance?

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Straight line → ruler. Curved line → pair of dividers or string.
Ground distance = map distance × the number in the scale.

cards.title: Area on a map
body: You know the area formula for squares and rectangles from geometry.
In social studies we use the same formula. But first we **convert map distance to ground distance**.

cards.title: Three steps
body: **1.** Measure the two sides. This is the map distance.
**2.** Convert the map distance to ground distance.
**3.** Multiply the two sides. This gives the **ground area**.

cards.title: Example 1: a square
cards.problem: A square has sides of 2 cm on a map. The scale is 1 cm to 5 km. Find the ground area.

steps.text: Each side is 2 cm (map distance).

cards.title: Example 2: a rectangle
cards.problem: A rectangle is 2 cm by 4 cm on a map. The scale is 1 cm to 8 km. Find the ground area.

cards.title: Try it: a square of 4 cm
cards.problem: The sides of a square are 4 cm each. The scale is 1 cm to 8 km. What is the ground area?

cards.title: Careful!
body: **Convert first, then multiply.**
Do not multiply 2 × 2 = 4 and then 4 × 5. That gives 20, which is wrong. The right answer is 100 km².

cards.q: A square has sides of 3 cm. The scale is 1 cm to 8 km. What is the ground area?

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Area: measure → convert → multiply.
Area is in **square kilometres** (km²).

units.title: Population
units.intro: In this unit you learn what population is, why people live close together in some places, how to calculate density and growth, and how to solve the problems of fast growth.

rni.title: Birth and death rates by continent

cards.title: Population
body: **Population** means the number of people living in a place.
- The population of Asmara is the number of people living in Asmara.
- **National population** is the total population of a country.
- **World population** is the total population of the earth.

cards.title: Demography
body: The study of population is called **demography**. It studies:
- the **size**, **composition** and **distribution** of the population of an area;
- how these change over time through birth rate, death rate and migration;
- the **results** of these changes.

steps.text: **Birth rate** is the number of births per 1000 people per year. Births add people.
**Death rate** is the number of deaths per year. Deaths take people away.
**Immigrants** are people who enter one country from another country.
**Emigrants** are people who leave their country and go to another country.

cards.title: Migration and census
body: **Migration** is the movement of people from place to place.
The official counting of the population of a region or a country is called a **census**.

cards.title: Name the arrows
body: Tap each dot. Green arrows add people. Red arrows take people away.

cards.title: Why study population?
body: The number of people has a big role in **economic development**.
If there is plenty of fertile land but few people, the land may stay **uncultivated**.
If the population grows much faster than crop production, there are many young children. They need food and schools.

cards.title: More children, more needs
body: Parents need more resources to feed, clothe and educate their children.
The government must build more schools and hospitals. It must employ more teachers and doctors.
This may **slow** economic development.

cards.title: Planning helps
body: Fast growth can be solved by **proper planning**:
- opening many **industries** where people can get jobs;
- using **modern farming**: fertilizers, insecticide, selected seeds, irrigation and soil conservation.

cards.title: Eritrea's plans
body: Many small **dams** are being built. **Terracing** and soil conservation happen everywhere.
Farmers use **irrigation** and get selected seeds. Cotton areas are expanding.
**Horticulture** (growing fruits and vegetables) is expanding fast. **Poultry** is growing very fast.

cards.title: Eritrea and growth
body: In Eritrea, population growth is **encouraged**. It helps the country to have a large **labour force**.
If growth is high, it can be solved by good farming and industry plans.

cards.title: Memory trick: B-D-M
body: Real population change depends on **B**, **D** and **M**.

cards.q: People who leave their country and go to another country are called:
cards.why: **E**migrants **e**xit. **I**mmigrants come **i**n.

cards.title: Two words
body: **Density of population** means the number of people living in one square kilometre.
**Distribution of population** means how people are spread across a country, a continent or the whole earth.

cards.title: People are not spread equally
body: More than **half** of the world's people live in **Asia**. But Asia has only one-fifth of the world's land.
In Eritrea, the **highlands** are more densely populated than the **lowlands**.

cards.title: Low and high density
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Low
states.text: **Low density areas** have fewer than **20 people** per square kilometre. Large areas of the world are like this.

states.label: High
states.text: **High density areas** have more than **250 people** per square kilometre on average (p. 18).

cards.title: Why? Natural resources
body: The distribution of population depends on the **amount and quality of natural resources**.

cards.title: Low density 1: cold areas
body: Polar regions, the **tundra** and high mountains are very cold. The temperature is below 0 °C.
They are covered with snow for most of the year. They are not good for crops, so few people live there.
Examples: northern Europe, northern Asia, northern Canada and Antarctica.

cards.title: High mountains
body: Cold high mountains include the Rockies, Andes, Alps, Himalayas, Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya.
**Dry areas** also have low density, because the rain is not enough for crops.

cards.title: Low density 2: rocky and hilly areas
body: Steep, rocky and hilly areas have **poor soil** because of erosion.
Example: the eastern escarpment south of Ghinda'e is steep, with no plants and poor soil. Very few people live there.

cards.title: Low density 3: hot deserts
body: Tropical hot deserts get less than **254 mm** of rain a year. The soil is poor.
Evaporation is more than the rainfall. So farming is difficult, and density is very low.
Big hot deserts: **Sahara**, **Namib**, **Atacama** and the Australian Desert.

cards.title: But water changes everything
body: Where there is plenty of water, like the **Nile river**, the density is more than **1000 people** per square kilometre.

cards.title: High density: why?
body: A place may have high density if it has:
- flat and fertile land;
- plenty of minerals;
- a good climate for crops and for people;
- industry and good transport.

cards.title: Main high density areas
head: Continent
Areas
rows: The Nile Valley, coastal West Africa

cards.title: Where do people live?
body: Tap each dot. Which places have many houses?

cards.q: Why is the tundra sparsely populated?
cards.why: The tundra is very cold and covered with snow for most of the year. Crops cannot grow.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Low density: cold, dry, rocky or hilly, hot desert.
High density: flat fertile land, minerals, good climate, industry.

cards.title: You need two numbers
body: To calculate the population density of a country you need:
- the **total area** in square kilometres;
- the **total population**.

cards.title: The formula
cards.problem: How do we find population density?

steps.text: Divide the **people** by the **area**. Not the other way round!

cards.answer: Density = population ÷ area, in persons per km².

cards.title: Example: Singapore in 2005
cards.problem: Singapore had 4,425,720 people and a land area of 685 km² in 2005. Find the density.

cards.title: Try it: an area of 1000 km²
cards.problem: An area has 25,000 people. Its area is 1000 km². What is the average density?

steps.text: Density = people ÷ area.

cards.title: Try it: Eritrea in 2005
cards.problem: Eritrea had about 4,561,599 people in 2005. Its area is 124,330 km². What was the density?

cards.title: Try it: Gambia
cards.problem: Gambia has an area of 11,000 km² and 902,089 people. What is the density?

steps.text: Density = people ÷ area.

cards.q: A country has 1 million people and an area of 1000 km². What is the density?

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Density = **people ÷ area**.
The answer is in persons per square kilometre.

cards.title: Population always changes
body: **Population size** means the number of people. It always changes.
The real changes depend on **birth rate**, **death rate** and **migration**.

cards.title: Rate of natural increase (RNI)
body: The **rate of natural increase** is the birth rate minus the death rate, per 1000 people per year.
We use it when no immigrants or emigrants move in or out.

cards.title: Example: RNI
cards.problem: Suppose the birth rate in Eritrea is 50 per 1000 and the death rate is 20 per 1000. Find the RNI.

cards.title: Try it: RNI
cards.problem: The birth rate is 30 per 1000 and the death rate is 10 per 1000. What is the RNI?

cards.title: Try it: a town
cards.problem: In a town the birth rate is 40 per 1000 and the death rate is 25 per 1000. What is the RNI?

cards.title: Birth and death rates
body: Green bars are birth rates. Red bars are death rates. The gap between them is the RNI.

cards.title: Read the table
body: **Africa** has the highest birth rate, the highest death rate and the highest RNI.
**Europe** has the lowest birth rate and the lowest RNI.

cards.q: Which continent has the highest RNI in the table?
cards.why: Africa: 4.0 − 1.5 = 2.5. That is the biggest RNI in the table.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: **RNI = BR − DR**.
Real change = births, deaths **and** migration.

cards.title: The world grows fast
body: At present the world population is growing very fast. This brings problems.

cards.title: Problem 1: limited resources
body: Oil, coal, natural gas and other minerals may be **finished** soon.
Land becomes **over-cultivated** and **over-grazed**. Soil fertility and crop yields go down.
This leads to **starvation** and **migration**.

cards.title: Solutions to problem 1
body: Wind, tidal, thermal and solar energy can replace oil, coal and gas.
Fertilizers can make the soil fertile again. Fewer, better animals can stop over-grazing.
Mountains can be **terraced**. Swamps can be drained and farmed.

cards.title: Problem 2: moving to towns
body: Landless and jobless people move from the countryside to towns to look for work.
It is hard to find food, jobs and houses. This leads to unrest and crime, like theft.

cards.title: Problem 3: the environment
body: Fast growth also causes **deforestation** and **soil erosion**. Careless tree cutting adds to it.
This can be solved by **reforestation** (planting trees again).

cards.title: Problem → solution
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Resources
states.text: Resources run out → use other energy and fertilizers.

states.label: Towns
states.text: People crowd into towns → build industries to give jobs.

states.label: Environment
states.text: Deforestation and erosion → plant trees and make terraces.

cards.title: Solution A: more farm products
body: - Get more from land already farmed: fertilizers, insecticides, irrigation, crop rotation, fallowing, mulching.
- Open new farm land: irrigate dry areas and drain swamps.

cards.title: Solutions B and C
body: **B. Migration:** some countries move people from crowded areas to empty areas that are rich in resources.
**C. Industrialisation:** industries give jobs. Refineries make kerosene, so less fuel wood is needed. Chemical industries make fertilizers.

cards.q: Which is NOT a problem of fast population growth?
cards.why: Conservation protects resources. It is a solution, not a problem.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Three solutions: **more farm products**, **migration** to empty rich areas, **industries**.

units.title: People and the Environment
units.intro: In this unit you learn what the environment is and about today's big environmental problems: global warming, the ozone hole, air and water pollution, and less groundwater.

pins.text: Lakes and seas polluted, life dies

cards.title: The environment
body: The **environment** is the surroundings in which we live. It means anything around us.
It is made up of many things. We call them **features** or **components** of the environment.

cards.title: Two kinds of components
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Physical
states.text: Air, trees, hills, rivers, animals, minerals and water form **naturally**. They are **physical components**. They make the physical or natural environment.

states.label: Human
states.text: Buildings, roads, factories, playgrounds and farmland are **man-made**. They are **human components**. They make the human or cultural environment.

cards.title: Physical or human?
body: Tap each dot to name the component.

cards.title: Not the same everywhere
body: Components are unevenly spread on the earth.
Tropical rainforest has dense forests. Savannah has grass. Deserts have few trees and animals. Coasts are rich in sea life.

cards.title: People respond to their environment
body: In a **cold** place people wear thick clothes, use fire and turn on heaters.
In a **hot** place people wear light clothes and use air conditioners.

cards.title: Good and bad effects of people
head: Positive
Negative
rows: Farmers clear land and get enough food
Mountains are terraced to get more farmland
Less fuel wood and less groundwater

cards.title: New problems
body: You already know deforestation, soil erosion, water pollution, flooding and drought.
Other problems made by people are **global warming**, **ozone depletion**, **air and water pollution** and **shortage of groundwater**.
**Deplete** means to become less in amount.

cards.q: Which is a human component of the environment?
cards.why: A factory is man-made. Rivers, mountains and the atmosphere are natural.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Physical = natural (air, trees, rivers). Human = man-made (roads, buildings, farms).
People's activities have both **positive** and **negative** effects.

lessons.title: Global Warming and the Ozone Layer

cards.title: What is global warming?
body: **Global warming** is the increase of the average temperature of the atmosphere.
Today the earth's temperature is rising very fast. This is partly because of human activities.

cards.title: Gases in the air
body: The atmosphere has nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
**Water vapour** and **carbon dioxide** warm the atmosphere. They keep the earth's average temperature steady.
If their amounts change, the temperature changes too.

steps.text: The sun gives off heat called **solar radiation**. It passes through the atmosphere without heating it.
It strikes the earth's surface and changes into **heat**.
Normally, heat goes back up and some of it escapes to outer space.
With too much carbon dioxide and water vapour, the heat is **trapped** in the lower atmosphere. The earth gets warmer.

cards.title: Causes
body: **a. Burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas). Factories, cars, buses and trucks release smoke full of carbon dioxide.
**b. Burning wood, charcoal, dung and shrubs** at home for cooking.
**c. Deforestation.** Green plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. With fewer plants, more carbon dioxide stays in the air.

cards.title: How much warmer?
body: The earth's average temperature is about **15 °C**.
In the last century it rose by **0.6 °C**, because carbon dioxide has increased greatly.
Scientists predict it will rise more.

cards.title: Results of global warming
body: 1. **Polar ice caps melt.** The sea level rises and floods coasts and low islands.
2. Animals and plants find it hard to adjust. Animals move towards the poles and high mountains.
3. Many kinds of animals and plants will **disappear**.

cards.title: Results: health
body: 4. Warmer regions will expand. More people will get sick or die from the heat.
Mosquitoes will move to places that used to be cold. Tropical diseases will spread.
There will also be more breathing (respiratory) diseases.

cards.title: Memory trick: FWD
body: Global warming goes **F-W-D** (forward).

cards.title: The ozone layer
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Healthy
states.text: High up in the atmosphere is a layer of gas called **ozone**. It protects life by absorbing the sun's harmful **ultra-violet rays**.

states.label: Hole
states.text: Chemicals made by people make the layer thin and create **holes**. Ultra-violet rays then reach the earth's surface.

cards.title: Why ultra-violet rays are harmful
body: - They cause **skin cancer** and **blindness**.
- They make people less able to fight infections.
- They destroy **plankton** in the oceans. Plankton is important food for fish.

cards.q: Which is NOT a result of global warming?
cards.why: Ozone depletion is caused by chemicals. It is a separate problem, not a result of global warming.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Global warming: more CO₂ and water vapour trap heat.
Ozone hole: ultra-violet rays get through.

cards.title: What is air pollution?
body: There is **air pollution** when the atmosphere is spoiled by smoke and other particles.
Things like smoke that pollute the air are called **pollutants**.

cards.title: Where the smoke comes from
body: Factories, cars, lorries and airplanes burn fossil fuels.
The smoke has carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and other gases. These harm people, animals and plants.
Burning wood, charcoal and coal also pollutes the air.

cards.title: Three harmful things in smoke
head: Pollutant
What it does
rows: Headache, no appetite, tiredness; paralysis, mental problems, destroys brain cells
Less oxygen in the blood; headaches and tiredness
Joins with oxygen to make sulphuric acid, which forms acid rain

steps.text: Petrol and fuels burn and release **sulphur dioxide**.
The gas rises into the atmosphere.
It combines with oxygen to form **sulphuric acid**.
This falls as **acid rain**.

cards.title: Effects of acid rain
body: Tap each dot to see one effect.

cards.title: Air pollution in Eritrea
body: Air pollution is not a major threat in Eritrea.
But it is beginning in industrial cities like **Asmara** and **Massawa**, and in some villages.

cards.title: Preventing air pollution
body: Air is an important natural resource. We should:
1. reduce the smoke we release;
2. reduce the lead in petrol;
3. put **filters** on chimneys of kitchens, factories and power stations.

cards.q: What are the effects of acid rain?
cards.why: Acid rain harms soil, buildings, trees and lakes.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Sulphur dioxide + oxygen → sulphuric acid → **acid rain**.
Filters on chimneys reduce pollution.

cards.title: What is water pollution?
body: **Water pollution** is when streams, lakes, wells, underground water or oceans are spoiled by harmful substances.
Poison chemicals or harmful micro-organisms can harm people, plants and animals.
Fish from polluted water may be unsafe to eat.

cards.title: The major water pollutants
body: Tap each dot to see how people pollute water.

cards.title: Three major water pollutants
body: 1. **Sewage** (waste carried in pipes) and **garbage** from houses.
2. **Chemical waste** from factories and oil tankers (ships).
3. Chemical **fertilizers**, **pesticides**, **insecticides** and **herbicides**.

cards.title: Protecting water
body: 1. Collect garbage in special places. Never throw it into rivers or seas.
2. Keep water sources and the area around them clean.
3. Build toilets **away** from water sources.

cards.title: More ways to protect water
body: 4. Make separate drinking places for animals.
5. Spray less pesticide and insecticide on farms and gardens.
6. **Fence** water sources.

cards.title: Groundwater
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Rain
states.text: Water seeps down into the ground and is stored under the surface. This is **groundwater**. Springs and wells get their water from it.

states.label: Drought
states.text: When people use more water and droughts come, the water is not replaced. The groundwater goes **down**.

cards.title: Groundwater is important
body: Groundwater is used for drinking and farming.
In the USA, 50% of drinking water comes from groundwater. In Eritrea, it is a source of drinking water.

cards.title: Why Eritrea uses more groundwater
body: Use has grown since independence because:
1. **horticulture** is growing fast;
2. new villages and towns need water;
3. many wells have been dug in villages;
4. more factories need water.

cards.title: Why it is running short
body: Demand is growing, and **droughts** happen often.
In tropical countries like Eritrea, rain is small and irregular. The used water is not replaced.

cards.q: Where does the water of springs and wells come from?
cards.why: The water in springs and wells comes from groundwater.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Water pollutants: sewage and garbage, chemical waste, farm chemicals.
Groundwater falls because of **overuse** and **drought**.

units.title: Communication
units.intro: In this unit you learn what communication is, the many ways people express messages, and how communication grew from sounds and gestures to e-mail.

pins.text: Road sign: a message to drivers

cards.title: What is communication?
body: **Communication** means sharing or passing information, ideas, feelings, opinions, orders and instructions.
It is also the **sending and receiving of messages**. It is a two-way sharing of information.

steps.text: There is a **message**: an idea, a feeling or some information.
The **sender** sends the message.
The **receiver** gets it and can send a reply. Communication goes **two ways**.

cards.title: Communication includes
body: 1. **Talking**, and **non-verbal** communication: a happy or sad face, or a gesture like saluting.
2. **Writing**.
3. Telephone calls, mail, pictures, video and television.

cards.title: Why it matters
body: Communication is an important part of personal life.
It is useful in **business**, in **education** and when people meet each other.

cards.q: Why is smiling a kind of communication?

options.B: It passes a feeling without words

cards.why: A smile is non-verbal communication. It shows happiness or satisfaction.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Communication = sending **and** receiving messages.
Non-verbal = without words: faces and gestures.

cards.title: People communicate in many ways
body: 1. A **drum** is beaten to call people to gather.
2. **Yawning** shows lack of sleep or tiredness.
3. **Laughing or smiling** shows happiness or satisfaction.

cards.title: More ways
body: 4. **Chatting** or **group discussion** at work or at a meeting shares ideas.
5. **Speaking**: when one person talks, the other listens.
6. **Road signs** and **notices** pass messages to others.

cards.title: What does each one say?
body: Tap each dot to see the message.

cards.title: Why we communicate
body: We need to know what is going on in our community, our country and the world.
We communicate all the time with family, friends, teachers and others. When teachers teach and pupils learn, that is communication too.

cards.q: Which is an example of non-verbal communication?
cards.why: A facial expression passes a message without words.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Drums, yawns, smiles, talking and road signs all pass messages.

cards.title: Sounds and gestures
body: Early people communicated by **sounds** and **gestures** before they had words.
The sounds were like the barking of dogs. The gestures were like moving the hands.
Later these developed into **words**.

cards.title: A problem with spoken messages
body: Messages carried by mouth from person to person to far places were **not passed correctly**.
Animals carried the messenger from village to village.

steps.text: First **sounds and gestures**, then **words**.
**Paintings and drawings** were the first steps towards writing. Then came **writing**.
**Messengers**, then the **postal service**.
**1876** the telephone; **1895** the radio.
Television and newspapers. The fastest: **fax, telegram, telex and e-mail**.

cards.title: Old pictures in Eritrea
body: Eritrea has many ancient paintings and drawings.
- Drawings of animals around **Kesekese**.
- Paintings in villages around **Adi Keih**.
- **Inscriptions** on the stelae of **Belew Kelew** at Metera. They are difficult to understand.

cards.title: Why writing helped
body: Writing made communication easy and **reliable**:
1. Written messages could be sent to far places.
2. Writing helped to **record** information.

cards.q: Before language, early people communicated by:
cards.why: Early people used sounds and gestures before they developed words.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Sounds and gestures → words → drawing and painting → writing.

cards.title: A. Postal service
body: The earliest message service was **messengers**. They carried memorised or written messages and came back with the reply.
The postal service is more important than messengers. It is **secure**, and the post office takes responsibility.

steps.text: **1.** Write a letter.
**2.** Put the letter in an envelope.
**3.** Write the postal address on the envelope.
**4.** Buy a stamp at the post office and put it on.
**5.** Put the envelope into a letter box.
**6.** A car carries it to where your friend lives.
**7.** The postman puts it in the correct letter box.
**8.** Your friend gets the letter and reads it.

cards.title: B. Newspapers
body: Newspapers are a very important means of communication. Their purpose is like radio and television.
We get current news, sports and historical events from newspapers.

cards.title: C. Telephone
body: A **telephone** sends and receives **voice** messages. You dial the number, and the other person picks up the receiver.
It is one of the **fastest** ways of sending messages: a few seconds to another town or country.
It was invented in **1876** by Alexander Graham Bell, a Scotsman in the USA.

cards.title: D. Radio
body: Radio sends news, music, discussions and interviews to any part of the world from a radio station.
Its most common use is **broadcasting news**.
An Italian scientist, **Guglielmo Marconi**, invented radio in **1895**.

cards.title: E. Television
body: Television shows **moving pictures** and news to **millions** of people at the same time.
People learn about people, places and things in far countries by watching it.

steps.text: Put the message or picture into the machine. Both people need fax machines, joined to telephone lines.
Dial the fax number of the other person.
A copy comes out of the other person's fax machine **immediately**.

cards.title: G. Telegram and H. Telex
body: **Telegram:** write your message on a special form at the post office. Codes (signals) for each word go along a single wire. It was invented by the American **Samuel F. B. Morse**.
**Telex:** an office worker types on a special typewriter. The receiver reads it on their telex machine.

cards.title: I. E-mail
body: **E-mail** (electronic mail) sends messages and data from one computer to another over the **internet**, very quickly.
In Asmara, people go to **internet cafés** to send and receive messages.

Fax, telegram, telex and e-mail are the fastest.

units.title: Social Development: Primitive Communal to Feudalism
units.intro: In this unit you learn how human society developed from a lower to a higher stage: from the Primitive Communal System, to Slave Society, to Feudalism.

cards.title: Basic needs today
body: Today most people live in houses in cities, towns and villages.
They buy what they need. Food, drink, shoes and clothes are **basic needs**.

cards.title: Long ago
body: People lived in open areas and forests. They did not know how to grow crops.
They moved from place to place looking for eggs, fruits and roots. They ate mainly plants.
They had no houses. This stage is called the **Primitive Communal System**.

steps.text: **Fire**: people could cook food, eat better and more kinds of food, keep warm and frighten animals away.
**Bow and arrow**: better hunting. Meat helped build up their bodies.
Animals caught in hunting were kept. This led to **domestication of animals**: meat, milk, and skins and bones for tools.
**Metals**: stronger tools like ploughs and axes, and weapons like knives and spears.
People learned crops could be grown. **Farming** started. Better tools and **irrigation** gave more crops.
People no longer had to wander. They built **permanent houses** and lived in communities.

cards.title: Name the development
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: What is a community?
body: A **community** is made up of people who live together in one area.
People in a community have **common needs and interests**.

cards.title: New jobs
body: With better ploughs and irrigation, **fewer people** were needed to grow crops.
The rest could do other work, like making **crafts** (pots, cotton-spinning) and **trade**.

cards.title: Sharing at first
body: In the early communities there were no differences between people. There were **no rich and no poor**.
People **shared** what they collected or hunted.

cards.title: Then private property
body: Better tools made more things. Individual work started.
People kept food and crafts for themselves. These became **private property**.

steps.text: Better tools and new techniques gave **more crops**.
Fewer farmers were needed, so others turned to **crafts and trade**.
People kept things for themselves: **private property**.
Some had more than others. Traders made profits. **Differences in wealth** grew.
This led to the emergence of **classes**.

cards.title: What is a class?
body: People who belong to the same group in society form a **class**.
They may do the same work, have the same income or the same social position.

cards.title: Classes in ancient times
body: Tap each level, from top to bottom.

cards.q: In the earliest Primitive Communal System, were there classes?
cards.why: There were no rich and poor people. People shared what they had.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Fire, bow and arrow, animals, metals, farming → communities.
Private property + wealth differences → **classes**.

cards.title: The first class society
body: People now had more food than they needed to survive. So they could keep **slaves**.
People who kept slaves were called **slave owners**.
**Slave Society** was the first society with classes. Most work was done by slaves.

cards.title: The classes
body: The main classes were **slave owners** and **slaves**.
There were also some **free farmers** and **craftsmen**.

cards.title: How did free people become slaves?
body: 1. People who could **not pay their debts** had to work without pay. In the end they became slaves.
2. **Prisoners of war** became slaves.
Slaves had **no rights** and **no property**.

cards.title: The caste system
body: Some countries developed the **caste system**. Society was divided into levels.
Each level had people of the same occupation, social position and influence.

cards.title: The caste system in India
body: Priests at the top, servants and workers at the bottom.

cards.title: Born into it
body: Ancient **India** had the caste system. The slave society of ancient **Sparta** was based on it too.
Positions were **inherited**. The sons of warriors became warriors.

cards.q: Which was NOT a way to become a slave?
cards.why: Debt and war made people slaves. Slave owners were the ones who kept slaves.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Slave Society = the first class society.
Classes: slave owners, slaves, free farmers and craftsmen.

cards.title: Why the slave system declined
body: Slaves had no rights or property, so they were **not satisfied**. They became less and less useful.
To make them work better, landowners gave them land.

steps.text: Slaves were given land. In return they worked the landowner's land and paid taxes. They became **serfs**.
There was no strong government, so there was a lot of fighting. Small farmers asked local lords for protection and lost their land. They became **tenants**.
Both worked the lord's fields and paid taxes. This is how **feudalism** appeared.

cards.title: Serf or tenant?
head: Serf
Tenant
rows: Could not leave; sold with the estate

cards.title: Feudal administration
body: Big landlords became **rulers** of their areas. Their duties were:
- defending the area against enemies;
- keeping law and order.
There was **no central government**. A central government has effective control of an area or country.

cards.title: Different kinds of feudalism
body: Places differed in location, culture and tradition, so feudalism took different forms.
In **Europe**, where there was much land, feudalism was based on **land**.
In some countries of **Africa**, it was based on **cattle** ownership.

cards.title: Three stages
body: Move the slider to climb the stages.

units.intro: In this unit you learn how government began, what government does, the three branches of government, centralized and decentralized systems, and Regional Administration in Eritrea.

clans.title: From people to clans to tribes

cards.title: No government at first
body: Early people were hunters and wanderers. They collected roots, fruits and eggs, and hunted animals.
There was not enough food for big groups to live together. People lived separately.
So they could not have a common organisation.

steps.text: At first people lived **separately**.
People who lived close together and talked with each other formed **clans**.
Clans joined together to form **tribes**.

cards.title: Tribal government
body: The **oldest** form of government was that of ancient clans and tribes. It can also be called **administration**.
These communities had **no classes**. So the government led the community in the **common interest**.

cards.title: Shared needs
body: The people had similar interests:
a. the need for **land** (owned and used jointly);
b. **protection** from enemies.
There was no difference in wealth.

cards.title: What did clan leaders organise?
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Clan and tribal leaders
body: Leaders coordinated hunting, farming, looking after cattle and defending the community.
They followed the laws of **tradition or custom**.
Leaders were **appointed** and could be **removed**.

cards.q: Why did tribal government lead in the common interest?
cards.why: The communities had no classes and no differences in wealth. So leaders worked for everyone.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: People → clans → tribes.
Tribal leaders were appointed and could be removed.

cards.title: Why government changed
body: Better tools let people work without help. They kept things for themselves and sold the rest.
This led to **differences in wealth** and to class societies like Slave and Feudal Society.
So government was needed to **protect the property of the rich**.

cards.title: City-states
body: At first, government covered small areas like cities. They were called **city-states**.
Ancient Greece had Athens, Sparta, Corinth and Thebes.
Ancient **Eritrea** had city-states such as **Adulis**, **Coloe** and **Toconda**.

cards.title: Democracy in Athens
body: In ancient Athens there was **rule by the people**, called **democracy**.
The population was small, so all the people took part **directly** in government.

cards.title: Government grows
body: Move the slider.

states.label: City-state
states.text: At first a government ruled only one city.

states.label: Nation
states.text: Cities grew stronger and expanded. Trade joined communities. Today we have **national governments** for whole countries.

cards.title: What is government?
body: **Government** is a body which **controls and coordinates** activities in society.

cards.title: Duties of government
body: Tap each dot to see a duty.

steps.text: **Legislature**: the law-making body.
**Judiciary**: the courts.
**Executive**: makes decisions and runs daily affairs by law (e.g. President, Prime Minister).

cards.title: Why separate powers?
body: **Separation of powers** means several branches share the task of government.
It stops one body or branch from becoming **too strong**.

cards.q: Which branch makes laws?
cards.why: The legislature is the law-making body. The judiciary is the courts.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Three branches: **legislature** (laws), **judiciary** (courts), **executive** (decisions).
Separation stops one branch getting too strong.

cards.title: Two systems
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Centralized
states.text: The **national government has overall authority**. Regions may have some powers. This is a **unitary state**.

states.label: Decentralized
states.text: The national and regional governments **share** some basic powers. The regions have their **own governments**. This is a **federal** system.

cards.q: Which country has a decentralized (federal) system?
cards.why: The book names the United States and India as federal. Eritrea, France and the UK are unitary.

cards.title: Remember this!

cards.title: Eritrea: a unitary state
body: Eritrea has a **central government** which decides all major policies and plans.
Eritrea also has **Regional Administration**. It gives local areas much freedom.

cards.title: Who does what?

The **Regions** carry them out.

cards.title: Why Regional Administration?
body: - to encourage **local initiative** and carry out needed programmes;

cards.title: Smaller units

units.title: Natural Heritages in Eritrea
units.intro: In this unit you learn what heritage is, and about Eritrea's natural heritages: the Red Sea, corals, sea grass, mangroves, sea animals and birds, and land plants and animals.

pins.text: Turtle: a reptile with a shell

trees.title: Trees of the lowlands and highlands

cards.title: Heritage
body: **Heritage** means something passed from the past to the present.
It can be **cultural heritage** or **natural heritage**.

cards.title: Two kinds of heritage
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Cultural
states.text: **Culture**: beliefs, rules of behaviour, language, religion, art, dress, cooking, traditional dances and songs. Also monasteries, mosques, stelae and crafts.

states.label: Natural
states.text: **Natural heritage** is inherited in its **natural state**: wild animals, plants, minerals, soil, air, and the sea.

cards.title: Cultural heritage in Eritrea
body: Eritrea is rich in music, story telling, crafts, archaeological sites, architecture, sports, dress and foods.
Historical sites include **Adulis**, **Kohaito**, **Metera**, **Keskese** and **Tekondae**.

cards.title: Monasteries and mosques
body: There are **over 20** historical monasteries and several mosques.
The largest are **Debre Bizen**, **Hamm**, **Debre Sina**, and the **Shek Hamal** and **Sihaba** mosques in Massawa.
These places attract tourists and help the national economy.

cards.title: Crafts
body: Wood carving, pottery, jewellery, painting, musical instruments and basketry are also cultural heritage.
They are important tourist attractions too.

cards.q: Which is a cultural heritage?
cards.why: A monastery was built by people. Coral, dolphins and the Red Sea are natural.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Cultural = made by people (sites, crafts, songs).
Natural = from nature (plants, animals, sea).

lessons.title: Natural Heritage and the Red Sea

cards.title: Natural heritage
body: Natural heritage in Eritrea includes geological places, plants and animals, marine resources and beautiful landscapes.

cards.title: Why the Red Sea is a heritage (1)
body: 1. It gives **salt** and sea animals: fish, whale, dolphin, dugong, lobster and shrimps.
There are **over 1000 kinds of fish**. **20%** of them are not found anywhere else in the world.
2. It gives Eritrea **access to the world**.

cards.title: Why the Red Sea is a heritage (2)
body: 3. Geothermal energy and tidal waves can make **electricity**.
4. It is rich in **sea grass** and **sea weed**, the homes and food of sea animals.
5. It has ports for import and export.

cards.title: The Eritrean Red Sea
body: Tap each dot. The map is simplified.

cards.title: Ports
body: Major ports: **Massawa** and **Assab**.
Small ports: Marsa Ibrahim, Marsa Mubarek, Marsa Teklay, Marsa Gulbub, Marsa Kubae and others.

cards.q: About what share of Red Sea fish kinds are found nowhere else?
cards.why: The book says 20% of the more than 1000 kinds are not found in other parts of the world.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Red Sea: salt, fish, access to the world, energy, sea plants, ports.

cards.title: Marine habitats
body: Coastal and marine heritage includes **coral reefs**, **sea grasses**, **sea weeds** and **mangrove forests**, and sea animals.
These are the living and breeding places (**habitats**) of sea animals. They are linked to each other.

cards.title: Name the habitat
body: Tap each dot.

steps.text: Tiny sea creatures called **polyps** live in warm, clear, shallow tropical sea.
When polyps die, their remains build up.
This forms **coral**, which is **limestone**. Corals vary in size and colour.

cards.title: Corals in Eritrea
body: Corals are common in the Red Sea. Most islands and coasts are rich in corals.
There are **5 new types** of coral in the Eritrean Red Sea not found anywhere else.

cards.title: Why corals matter
body: - They are homes of many sea plants and animals.
- They are used to make **beads** and ornaments. Local people sell them to tourists.
- They protect the coast from **wave erosion**.

cards.title: B. Sea grass
body: Sea grasses are **flowering plants** in shallow water. Their beds look like grassland.
They grow densely in the **southern** part of Eritrea's Red Sea.
They protect the sea bed from erosion. They feed fish, dugong and turtle, and shelter fish, shrimp and birds.

cards.title: Sea weeds
body: Sea weeds are marine plants (**algae**). They grow in sandy soils and on coral in shallow water.
They grow along the whole coast, but more in the south.
They give food and shelter to sea animals, and food to people.

cards.title: C. Mangrove forests
body: Mangroves are short shrubs; some trees grow to 25 metres. In Eritrea they grow to about **6 metres**.
They grow in coastal water. They are **salt-tolerant** and use sea water for water and nutrients.

cards.title: Why mangroves matter
body: 1. They protect the coast from wave erosion.
2. They are homes and food for sea animals and birds.
3. Camels eat them.
4. Their wood is light and does not rot, so it is used for boats and houses.
5. They give fuel wood.

cards.title: D. Fish
body: The **Dahlak Archipelago**, then **Hawakil Bay**, are richest in fish diversity. They have coral reefs, sea grass and sandy bottoms.
Fish are exported to **Europe**, the **Middle East** and the **Far East**.

cards.title: Where are the sea animals?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Fish
states.text: The Dahlak Archipelago is richest in fish, followed by Hawakil Bay.

states.label: Dugong
states.text: Dugongs live from Marsa Ibrahim to Ingel, from Nora to the Harmil islands (Dahlak), and around Assab. The map circles Dahlak and Assab.

states.label: Turtle
states.text: Turtles are hunted between **Thio and Assab**. They are endangered and should not be hunted.

cards.title: Marine animals
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Dugong
body: A dugong is a huge sea **mammal** (mammals feed their young with milk). It is also called the **sea cow**.
It is slow and eats plants. It is **endangered**: its number has fallen so much that it is almost extinct.
Uses: food, and its hide makes quality leather and shields.

cards.title: Turtle
body: A turtle is a **reptile** that eats plants. Its body is covered with a shell.
Eritrea has the **green turtle**. There are about 250 species in the world and 5 in the Eritrean Red Sea.
Uses: food, income, and shells for ornaments.

cards.title: Whale
body: The whale is a huge warm-blooded sea mammal. It is the **largest animal in the world**.
It gives meat and oil. The oil is used for cooking, lamps, soap, margarine and lubricants.
Its liver gives vitamins A and D. Bones and flesh make fertilizer.

cards.title: Dolphin (Abu Salama)
body: Dolphins are fast-swimming mammals related to whales. They are warm-blooded.
The **bottlenose dolphin** is grey, up to 4 m long and about 650 kg.
Uses: meat for food, and oil as a lubricant.

cards.title: Marine birds
body: There are **over 514** bird species around the Eritrean Red Sea. About **109** (21%) are in the Dahlak Archipelago.
**Sea birds** live on the sea and feed on fish near the surface.
**Shore birds** live on beaches and muddy coasts and eat small creatures or plants.

cards.title: Visitors from far away
body: Birds are either **residents** or **immigrants**.
Immigrant birds come from as far as **Finland** in Europe. They come to the warm Red Sea in the cold northern season.

cards.q: Which of these is a slow-moving animal?
cards.why: The dugong is a slow-moving, plant-eating mammal. Dolphins are fast swimmers.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Mammals: dugong, whale, dolphin. Reptile: turtle.
Endangered: dugong and turtle.

cards.title: Many land habitats
body: Eritrea has forests, grasslands, deserts, semi-deserts, coastal land and escarpment.
These are homes of many kinds of plants and animals.

cards.title: Lowland and highland trees
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Lowlands
states.text: **Acacia**, **baobab**, **palm** and **fig** trees grow mostly in the lowlands and at the foot of the escarpments.

states.label: Highlands
states.text: **Olive**, **fig**, **juniper** and **euphorbia** grow in the highlands.

states.label: Both
states.text: All these trees have **economic importance**.

cards.title: Wild animals
body: Baboon, African hedgehog, **Nubian ibex**, gazelle, dik-dik, **ostrich**, jackal, **wild ass**, **elephant**, hyena and greater kudu.
These animals attract tourists.

cards.title: Why fewer animals?
body: The number of wild animals has decreased because of:
- **droughts**;
- **expansion of agriculture**;
- the **thirty years of war**.

cards.q: Which tree commonly grows at the foot of the escarpments and in the lowlands?
cards.why: Baobab grows in the lowlands. Euphorbia, juniper and olive grow in the highlands.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Different environments → different trees and animals.
Animals fell because of drought, farming and war.

units.title: Disasters in Eritrea
units.intro: In this unit you learn what disasters are, and about the main disasters in Eritrea: drought, epidemics, pests, earthquakes, volcanoes and war.

tld.title: Timeline: drought, disease, pests and war

pins.text: Magma: molten rock inside the earth

cards.title: Disaster
body: A **disaster** is a sudden event that causes many deaths. Most disasters also damage property.
Some disasters are **natural**. Others are **man-made**.

cards.title: Major disasters in Eritrea
body: **Drought**, **earthquakes**, **volcanic eruptions**, **epidemics**, **pest infestation** and **war**.

cards.q: Which of these is a man-made disaster?
cards.why: War is caused by people. Earthquakes, volcanoes and drought are natural.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Disaster = sudden event, many deaths, property damage.

cards.title: Drought
body: **Drought** is a long, continuous dry period with little or no rain.
It causes famine, death and migration. Many animals die from lack of pasture and water.

steps.text: Little or no rain for a long time.
Low crop production and drying of streams.
Loss of livestock. In the 1985 drought, **60% to 70%** of Eritrea's livestock died.
Shortage of food.
Displacement of people and migration from villages to towns.

cards.title: Droughts in Eritrea
body: Droughts are frequent. There was drought and famine in 1913–1914 and in the early 1940s.
The **most serious** was in **1983–1984**. Thousands starved. In 1984/85 about **650,000** people were displaced, mostly lowland herders.
From 1970 to 1989 there were about **11 drought years**.

steps.text: **1888–1892**: famine caused by rinderpest.
**1913–1914** and the **early 1940s**: droughts and famine.
**1957**: locusts badly hit crop production.
**1961–1991**: the war for independence.
**1970–1989**: about 11 drought years. **1983–84**: the worst drought.
**1984–85**: about 650,000 displaced. **1988**: cholera, meningitis and malaria.

cards.title: Epidemics
body: An **epidemic** is the rapid spread of a disease among many people or livestock in the same place.
Examples are measles, cholera and influenza.
In Eritrea epidemics are **not** major national disasters. They happen in different places at different times.

cards.title: Examples
body: - **Cholera** broke out locally in 1973, 1987 and 1988.
- **Meningitis** in 1988.
- **Malaria** spread widely in 1988. It is common in the lowlands.
- **Measles** is common in many parts of Eritrea.

cards.title: Rinderpest famine (1888–1892)
body: The Italians brought in cattle, horses and mules infected with **rinderpest** through Massawa.
It killed about **90%** of Eritrea's cattle. The land could not be ploughed, so there was starvation.

cards.title: Pests
body: **Pests** are living things, like insects and weeds, that destroy plants, crops and stored grain.
The two major insect pests are **locusts** and **armyworms**. They destroy crops in the green stage.

cards.title: Locusts and armyworms
body: The **dry coastal areas** are good breeding grounds for locusts, so outbreaks may come again.
Locusts caused famine several times, and hit crops badly in **1957**.
Armyworms are becoming more common in recent years.

cards.q: The famine of 1888–1892 was caused by:
cards.why: Rinderpest killed about 90% of the cattle, so the land could not be ploughed.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Worst drought: **1983–84**.
Epidemics are local in Eritrea. Pests: locusts and armyworms.

cards.title: Earthquakes
body: **Earthquakes** are the shaking of the earth's surface.
They are caused by the movement of molten rocks inside the earth.
They are common in Eritrea, especially on the **coast**.

steps.text: **1400 AD**: Mount Dubbi (about 50 km south of Eddi) erupts, with earthquakes.
**1861**: Dubbi erupts again (June and September). 106 people and many herds are killed.
**Nov 1875 – Mar 1876**: earthquakes, worst around **Keren**. A landslide on Mt. Amba, 6 km west of Keren.
**20 July 1884**: Massawa is badly damaged; nearly all houses fall. A small **tsunami** follows.
**1901–02**: Mount Alid erupts. **1912–13**: earthquakes, worst in Massawa.
**1921**: the "year of earthquake". Massawa is largely destroyed (14 August and 21 September).
**20 August 1989**: an earthquake hits **Assab**. Bridges fall and a road is closed for a month.

cards.title: Thirty years of war
body: Eritreans fought for independence from Ethiopia from **1961 to 1991**.
Tens of thousands of Eritreans lost their lives. Livestock, infrastructure and the environment were damaged.

cards.title: Effects on people
body: People were wounded or killed. This reduced Eritrea's **productive force**.
The imprisonment of innocent people also reduced the working force.

cards.title: Effects on the environment
body: Forests were cut to build trenches and houses.
The Ethiopian army cut trees for fire-wood and charcoal. Wildlife was lost when forests were destroyed.

cards.title: Effects on services

Bridges, roads and dams were destroyed by the Ethiopian military.

units.title: Traditional Societies in Eritrea
units.intro: In this unit you learn about the traditional societies of the lowlands, the Sahil and the highlands of Eritrea: how they were organised, who led them, and how they lived.

pins.text: Tigre-speaking tribes: Sahil and northern plains
Bilen: Keren and the hills around

cards.title: The lowlands
body: The Eritrean lowlands are the **Western** and **Eastern** Lowlands.
The Western Lowlands have a north-western and a south-western part.
Long ago the north-western lowlands were settled by **Kushitic** and **Semitic** migrants. They mixed and formed many groups.

cards.title: Where do they live?
body: Tap each dot. The brown area is the highlands. The map is simplified.

cards.title: The Belaw
body: The **Belaw**, a Beja (Kushitic-speaking) group, were early people of this area. For a long time they were the rulers.
In the 16th century the Belaw came under the **Beni Amir Federation**.

cards.title: The Funj arrive
body: In the **16th century** the **Funj Kingdom** of Sennar (Sudan) expanded into Eritrea. The Belaw came under Funj control.
**Ali Abu Gassim**, an agent of the Funj, married the granddaughter of the Belaw king **Idris Mohammed Adera**. The Belaw killed him.

cards.title: The Federation is born
body: His son **Amir Ali Abu Gassim** was born after his death. He went to the Nile Valley, his father's home.
He came back with an army and defeated the Belaw.
He united the Beni Amir tribes into the **Beni Amir Federation**.

cards.title: How it was run
body: The Beni Amir had about **21 tribes**. Each tribe was divided into clans.
Clans looked after local matters. Higher chiefs (the **Omdas**) decided bigger matters.
The most important matters went to the **Diglal**, the paramount leader.

cards.title: Three castes
body: Tap each level.

cards.title: Serfs and slaves
head: Serfs
Slaves
rows: Could own cattle, sheep, goats, sometimes land

cards.title: Duties of the serfs
body: 1. Regular payments.
2. Gifts like goats and butter during visits.
3. Goats, bulls and help at funerals, weddings and births.
4. Camels for moving during seasonal migrations.
5. Looking after and milking cattle.

steps.text: The **Diglal** was the paramount (highest) chief of the nabtab tribes. He came from selected nabtab families.
**Omdas** were leaders at clan level.
**Sheiks** were leaders at the lowest level: the family or kinship group.

cards.title: Limits on power
body: The power of the Diglal was **limited** by his deputy, the **Sheik al-musheikh**.
A **clan council** settled clan problems.

cards.title: The Beni Amir today
body: Some clans speak **Tigre** and some speak **Bedhawyeet**.
The climate is dry, so most Beni Amir are **semi-nomadic**.
A few groups south-east of Agordat (Ad Sala, Ad Ali Bekhit and Tawliyab) became settled farmers.

cards.q: Who set up the Beni Amir Federation?
cards.why: Amir Ali Abu Gassim defeated the Belaw and united the Beni Amir tribes.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Castes: nabtabs, serfs, slaves.
Leaders: Diglal (tribes) → Omda (clan) → Sheik (family).

cards.title: Kunama and Nara
body: The **Nilotic** Kunama and Nara lived in the south-western lowlands.
They lived in small clans of a few hundred families, united by language and the need for protection.
There is enough rain and plenty of grass. Most are **farmers** who also raise cattle, goats and sheep.

cards.title: Women led
body: In early Kunama society, **women** had much influence and headed the community. This is a **matriarchal system**.
Ancestry was traced through the **mother**.

cards.title: Beliefs
body: The Kunama worshipped **Anna**, an invisible supernatural being. Anna created Adum and Aua (Adam and Eve).
This is the root of **ancestor worship** among the Kunama. The Nara also worshipped ancestors and nature.
Later the Nara adopted Islam. Some Kunama are Christians.

cards.title: Equal and democratic
body: Kunama and Nara societies were **democratic**: clan members were equal. There were no serfs and masters.
Matters were decided by **discussion**. Land was owned **collectively**.

cards.title: Change under Italy
body: By **1913** the Italian colonial administration appointed chiefs to control the local areas.
Chiefs ruled larger territories with more people.

cards.q: In early Kunama society, ancestry was traced through:
cards.why: It was a matriarchal system, so ancestry was identified through the mother.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Kunama and Nara: equal, democratic, land shared.
Kunama: matriarchal; worshipped Anna.

lessons.title: Eastern Lowlands, Sahil and Northern Plains

cards.title: Samhar
body: Kushitic and Semitic people have long lived here. They were semi-nomadic herders, and with Islam most became Muslim.
The major groups are the **Saho**, **Afar** and **Tigre**.

cards.title: Council of elders
body: The Saho and Afar of Samhar had **no master-serf** relations. A **council of elders** led each tribe.
The elders were elected democratically by custom.
Later Samhar came under the rule of the **Naib** family, who were of Belaw origin.

cards.title: Uses of animals in the lowlands
head: Use
Animals

cards.title: Dankalia
body: Many **Afars** live south-east of Samhar and on the islands near the coast.
They are Kushitic, speak Afar and are Muslim. Most are semi-nomadic. Some trade; others fish.
The book says these Afars have master-serf relations.

cards.title: The Sahil and northern plains
body: Kushitic (Beja) and Semitic people lived here. **Tigre-speaking** people were among the first.
Newcomers, the **Bet Asgede**, mixed with them. A caste system grew: an upper class (aristocracy) and serfs.

cards.title: Groups of the Sahil
head: Group
Way of life
rows: Red Sea coast; teachers of the Koran, then camels, sheep, goats
In the north, away from the coast; spoke Bedhawyeet; left the Beni Amir

cards.title: The Bilen
body: The **Bilen** (also called Bogos) live in **Keren** and the hills around it.
Their tribes are Gebre Tarke, Tauke and Bab Janjeren.
They are mainly farmers in small villages. Some are Muslim; others are Christian.

cards.q: Which Sahil group was democratic?
cards.why: The Ad Sawra were equal, could give their views, and chose their own leaders.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Samhar: Saho, Afar, Tigre; council of elders.
Bilen: Keren, mainly farmers.

cards.title: Farming came early
body: Settled farming was important in the highlands from early times.
Crops (millet, sorghum) and animal raising (goats, sheep, cattle) came from **Western Asia**.

steps.text: An **enda** was a number of families or kinship groups with the **same ancestor**.
Each family got land for ever. This land was called **risti**. Endas grew as people were born and migrants joined.
Common needs made endas join and form **villages**. Land belonged to the village and was shared: the **diessa** system.
Villages formed **districts**, with elected district chiefs (**meslenes**).

cards.title: Enda leaders
body: Endas were led by **elders**, elected democratically.
They collected taxes and acted as judges. Enda laws were based on custom.

cards.title: Gulti
body: Later a **feudal** structure, the **gulti**, appeared. A gulti was land granted by a ruler for special duties.
It did **not replace** the traditional structure. The diessa system became the most common.

cards.q: Land given permanently to families in the enda was called:
cards.why: Risti was given permanently. Diessa belonged to the village.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Enda → village → district.
Risti = family land. Diessa = village land.

cards.title: Feudal levels
body: Villages (**addi**) were grouped in clusters. A cluster of villages made a **gulti**.
Gultis formed a **medri** ("land"). Medris made up a district.
The smallest unit was the addi (village).

steps.text: The **shum-addi** headed the village. He collected taxes, kept his share and passed the rest up.
The **shum-gulti** kept his share and passed the rest to the medri official.
The **medri** head collected from the gultis, kept his share and sent the rest to the district head.
The **district ruler** was at the top.

cards.title: Why district administration?
body: Officials at every level also served as **judges**.
The aims were to **control** the district and to get **economic income** from it.

cards.title: Medieval settlements
body: The **medieval period** is the time between ancient and modern times, usually the time of feudalism.
Towns were few and small, but the countryside was densely populated. **Debarwa** town and **Tselot** village were well known.
Houses were low with flat roofs (possibly **hidmo**).

cards.title: A fertile land
body: Grains, grapes, oranges and peaches grew around the monastery of **Debre Bizen**.
Near Debarwa: wheat, barley, millet, chick-peas, lentils and vegetables. Also taff, dagusha and sorghum.
Mai Tsada grew a large amount of crops.

cards.title: Land and animals
body: Powerful local rulers, churches and monasteries owned land. Debre Bizen's lands were farmed by **tenants**.
People raised cattle, goats, sheep, donkeys and horses for more income.
Animals gave milk and meat, carried loads and pulled ploughs.

cards.title: Self-sufficient villages
body: Villages were **self-sufficient**: they made what they needed and used it there.
Things were not brought from outside, so there was little contact with other areas.
Peasants used oxen to plough. Villages made pottery, ground grain and wove cloth.

cards.title: A primary source: Alvarez
body: **Francisco Alvarez** visited in 1520–1527. He saw a **locust** invasion near Debarwa himself.
He wrote that "the sun became yellow". In another place, wheat, barley and tef looked as if never sown.
An eyewitness account like this is a **primary source**.

cards.q: What was the head of the village called in the feudal structure?
cards.why: The shum-addi headed the village (addi) and collected its taxes.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Addi → gulti → medri → district.
Highland villages were self-sufficient; people farmed and raised animals.
